A new energy function explicitly tailored to PI controller is proposed in this letter. It admits a unified form and can be applied to a class of nonlinear systems with PI controllers. Two representative cases are considered, including a grid-following (GFL) inverter and a DC-voltage-controlled grid-forming (GFM) inverter, demonstrating less conservative and more effective estimation of the region of attraction (ROA). All findings are verified through hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments.

AI.tldr: The letter proposes a new energy function tailored to PI controllers for transient stability analysis of inverter-based resources (IBRs), demonstrating less conservative region of attraction estimation for both grid-following and grid-forming inverters, validated by HIL experiments.
AI.motivation: Classical energy functions used for synchronous generators cannot be directly applied to IBRs with PI controllers due to fundamentally different nonlinear swing equations and state-dependent damping characteristics, necessitating a tailored energy function for accurate transient stability analysis.
AI.method: The authors derive a new energy function explicitly tailored to PI-controlled systems, which admits a unified form applicable to a class of nonlinear systems with PI controllers. The method is demonstrated on two representative cases: a grid-following (GFL) inverter and a DC-voltage-controlled grid-forming (GFM) inverter.
AI.result: The proposed energy function provides less conservative and more effective estimation of the region of attraction (ROA) compared to classical approaches. All findings are verified through hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) experiments.
AI.conclusion: The unified energy function tailored to PI controllers enables improved transient stability assessment for IBR-dominated power systems, offering a more accurate analytical tool than conventional energy function methods.

title: An Individual-Delay-Reflected Generalized Consensus Analysis for Multi-Agent Systems with Heterogeneous Time-Varying Delays
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures. Extended version of a paper accepted to IFAC World Congress 2026
summary: In multi-agent systems, heterogeneous time delays exist for all agents because of the difference in communication environments. Therefore, the consensus analysis of a system considering a homogeneous time-varying delay among all agents results in conservatism. In this study, an individual-delay-reflected generalized consensus is proposed for multi-agent systems with heterogeneous time-varying delays with various bounds. To reflect heterogeneous time-varying delays, the proposed Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional is constructed by dividing the integral term into intervals containing heterogeneous delays and considering augmented vectors with delay states and integral states. Furthermore, by adding zero equality conditions, conservatism is reduced. N-dependent generalized integral inequality is used to allow the user to adjust the computational complexity. Numerical examples demonstrate a reduction in conservatism with the proposed consensus criterion.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a less conservative consensus criterion for multi-agent systems with heterogeneous time-varying delays by constructing a specialized Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional that divides integral terms into intervals reflecting individual delays and using augmented vectors with delay/integral states, zero equality conditions, and N-dependent generalized integral inequalities.
AI.motivation: Existing consensus analyses assume homogeneous (identical) time delays across all agents, which introduces conservatism because in real multi-agent systems, communication environments differ, leading to heterogeneous time delays with various bounds.
AI.method: (1) Proposed an individual-delay-reflected generalized consensus formulation; (2) Constructed a Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional that divides the integral term into intervals containing heterogeneous delays; (3) Considered augmented vectors with delay states and integral states; (4) Added zero equality conditions to reduce conservatism; (5) Applied N-dependent generalized integral inequality to allow adjustable computational complexity.
AI.result: Numerical examples demonstrate a reduction in conservatism compared to approaches that assume homogeneous delays or use less refined bounding techniques.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach effectively reduces conservatism in consensus analysis of multi-agent systems by properly accounting for heterogeneous time-varying delays through customized Lyapunov-Krasovskii functional construction and advanced inequality techniques.

title: VLM-VPI: A Vision-Language Reasoning Framework for Improving Automated Vehicle-Pedestrian Interactions
comment: 40 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables
summary: Autonomous driving systems often infer pedestrian yielding behavior from geometric and kinematic cues alone, limiting their ability to reason about visual scene context and age-dependent behavioral variability. This limitation can produce delayed interventions in safety-critical encounters and unnecessary braking in benign interactions. This work introduces Vision-Language Model-based Vehicle-Pedestrian Interaction (VLM-VPI), a multimodal reasoning framework for pedestrian intent understanding and yielding-aware control in autonomous driving. The system combines three components: a multimodal perception layer that captures visual and kinematic observations, a reasoning layer that uses Qwen3-VL 8B for visual scene understanding and GPT-OSS 20B for few-shot intent reasoning, and a tiered safety controller that applies age-specific braking margins for children, adults, and seniors. In 112 CARLA scenarios, VLM-VPI achieves 92.3% intent classification accuracy, outperforming a rule-based baseline (78.4%), supervised trajectory models (73.5-82.4%), and a zero-shot LLM configuration (88.4%). Validation on 24 real-world PIE scenarios yields 87.5% accuracy, indicating functional sim-to-real transferability. Across 200 simulation cases, VLM-VPI reduces the false-alarm rate from 7.4% to 2.8% and mean intersection traversal time from 13.5 s to 11.8 s. Conflict occurrences decrease from 124 to 33, while mean minimum time-to-collision improves from 1.92 s to 4.47 s. Demographic-adaptive control further reduces conflicts by 60% for children and 54.5% for seniors compared with uniform control. These results show that an explicit vision-language reasoning layer can improve both safety and efficiency by linking pedestrian intent, demographic context, and vehicle control decisions.

AI.tldr: VLM-VPI is a multimodal reasoning framework using vision-language models (Qwen3-VL 8B + GPT-OSS 20B) for pedestrian intent prediction and age-adaptive braking control in autonomous driving. It achieves 92.3% intent accuracy in simulation and 87.5% in real-world PIE scenarios, reducing false-alarm rates from 7.4% to 2.8% and conflicts from 124 to 33, with demographic-specific control yielding 60% fewer conflicts for children and 54.5% for seniors.
AI.motivation: Current autonomous driving systems only use geometric/kinematic cues for pedestrian yielding inference, lacking visual scene context and age-dependent behavioral reasoning, leading to delayed interventions in safety-critical encounters and unnecessary braking in benign interactions.
AI.method: Three-component framework: (1) multimodal perception layer capturing visual and kinematic data, (2) reasoning layer combining Qwen3-VL 8B for scene understanding and GPT-OSS 20B for few-shot intent reasoning, (3) tiered safety controller applying age-specific braking margins for children, adults, and seniors.
AI.result: 112 CARLA scenarios: 92.3% intent accuracy (vs. 78.4% rule-based, 73.5-82.4% trajectory models, 88.4% zero-shot LLM). 24 PIE scenarios: 87.5% accuracy. 200 simulation cases: false-alarm rate 2.8% (down from 7.4%), traversal time 11.8 s (from 13.5 s), conflicts 33 (from 124), min TTC 4.47 s (from 1.92 s). Conflicts reduced 60% for children and 54.5% for seniors under demographic-adaptive control.
AI.conclusion: An explicit vision-language reasoning layer linking pedestrian intent, demographic context, and vehicle control can simultaneously improve both safety and efficiency in autonomous driving interactions.

title: Extracting Exact Lie Derivatives Without Backpropagation: A Dual Compiler for Neural Control Barrier Functions
summary: Deploying neural-network control barrier functions (CBFs) on embedded hardware requires evaluating the barrier value and its Lie derivatives along the system vector fields at every control cycle. The standard mechanism for exact gradient extraction, reverse-mode automatic differentiation, constructs a dynamic computational graph whose memory footprint grows with network depth and whose backward traversal obstructs the worst-case execution time analysis required for safety-critical certification. This paper presents a dual-algebraic compiler that extracts the exact barrier value and its Lie derivatives through forward network evaluation alone. Encoding the system state as the real part of a dual number and a target vector field as the dual part, we prove that every affine and componentwise-activation layer admits a dual extension that propagates the exact directional derivative alongside the activation, and that the composed dual-extended network evaluates the exact Jacobian--vector-field product with zero truncation error. We derive closed-form expressions for the dual-pass floating-point operation count and peak memory footprint, prove that the proposed algorithm eliminates dynamic graph allocation, and extend the framework to the second-order Lie derivatives required by relative-degree-two CBFs using hyper-dual arithmetic. An open-source ahead-of-time compiler translates trained neural CBFs into self-contained C++ headers that assemble the complete safety constraint on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller from a statically allocated buffer, with zero dynamic memory allocation and a sub-millisecond cycle budget that supports kilohertz-rate safety filters.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a dual-algebraic compiler that extracts exact barrier values and Lie derivatives from neural control barrier functions through forward network evaluation alone, eliminating dynamic computation graphs and enabling sub-millisecond safety filtering on embedded microcontrollers.
AI.motivation: Deploying neural CBFs on embedded hardware is hindered by reverse-mode automatic differentiation, which constructs dynamic computational graphs with memory footprints that grow with network depth and obstruct worst-case execution time analysis required for safety-critical certification.
AI.method: The authors develop a dual-algebraic compiler that encodes the system state as the real part of a dual number and the target vector field as the dual part. They prove that affine and componentwise-activation layers admit dual extensions that propagate exact directional derivatives alongside activations, and extend this to second-order Lie derivatives using hyper-dual arithmetic. The compiler translates trained neural CBFs into self-contained C++ headers with statically allocated buffers.
AI.result: The approach eliminates dynamic graph allocation, provides closed-form expressions for dual-pass FLOP count and peak memory footprint, and achieves sub-millisecond cycle budgets supporting kilohertz-rate safety filters on an ESP32-S3 microcontroller with zero dynamic memory allocation.
AI.conclusion: The dual-algebraic compiler enables certifiably safe, real-time deployment of neural CBFs on resource-constrained embedded hardware by replacing reverse-mode AD with forward dual-number propagation, eliminating dynamic memory allocation and enabling predictable worst-case execution time.

title: Safe Reconnection Time for Large-Scale Data Center Loads: An Analytical Framework for Transient Stability Assessment
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, accepted by PowerUp 2026
summary: The rapid growth of large, power-electronics-rich data center (DC) loads is creating new operational challenges for bulk power systems. A key risk arises when a DC uninterruptible power supply (UPS) disconnects the facility during voltage/frequency disturbances and then reconnects it while the bulk grid is still dynamically settling to a new equilibrium point. Poorly timed reconnection can amplify electromechanical oscillations, deepen frequency deviations, and lead to repeated connect-disconnect \emph{flapping}. In this paper, we develop an analytical framework to characterize the \emph{safe reconnection time} for large DC loads after a disturbance-induced disconnection that avoids flapping. Using a model in the spirit of the classical single-machine infinite-bus system, we capture (i) swing dynamics during the disconnection interval and (ii) voltage-angle coupling at the load bus, which determines the electrical power step at reconnection under constant-power load assumptions. Using energy function method, we characterize the critical safe reconnection time such that for any reconnection time after the critical safe reconnection time, the post-reconnection trajectory is guaranteed to remain within operational limits (frequency/angle/voltage) and converge to the post-reconnection equilibrium, thereby preventing flapping. Time-domain simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed analytical approach. The results provide a simple, physics-informed criterion that can be used to bound reconnection windows for large DC facilities and inform UPS reconnection logic.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an analytical framework to determine the safe reconnection time for large data center loads after disturbance-induced disconnection, using an energy function method on a single-machine infinite-bus model. It characterizes a critical safe reconnection time that guarantees post-reconnection stability and prevents repeated connect-disconnect flapping, validated through time-domain simulations.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of large, power-electronics-rich data center loads creates new operational challenges for bulk power systems. A key risk arises when a DC UPS disconnects the facility during disturbances and reconnects while the grid is still dynamically settling, which can amplify electromechanical oscillations, deepen frequency deviations, and lead to repeated connect-disconnect flapping. There is a need to characterize safe reconnection times to avoid these stability issues.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytical framework using a model in the spirit of the classical single-machine infinite-bus system, capturing (i) swing dynamics during the disconnection interval and (ii) voltage-angle coupling at the load bus determining the electrical power step at reconnection under constant-power load assumptions. They employ an energy function method to characterize the critical safe reconnection time.
AI.result: For any reconnection time after the critical safe reconnection time, the post-reconnection trajectory is guaranteed to remain within operational limits (frequency/angle/voltage) and converge to the post-reconnection equilibrium, thereby preventing flapping. Time-domain simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed analytical approach.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a simple, physics-informed criterion that can be used to bound reconnection windows for large DC facilities and inform UPS reconnection logic.

title: A Road-Mobile GNSS-Disciplined Oscillator for Accurate Synchronization of Vehicular Microwave Measurements
summary: Precise synchronization is essential in various technical disciplines, being especially challenging in mobile scenarios. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art global navigation satellite system (GNSS) disciplined oscillators (GNSSDOs) are designed and optimized for stationary operation. We present a novel solution that is optimized for mobile use from the ground up. The centerpiece is a precise oven-controlled crystal oscillator (OCXO) that is optimized for low sensitivity to dynamic accelerations. A state-of-the-art GNSS timing module is used to discipline it. We evaluate the system by comparing it with state-of-the-art test equipment in a real-world test drive through diverse environments. After compensating for the stationary offset, the state-of-the-art devices deviated by up to 2315 ns, while with our devices, the deviation never exceeded 22.6 ns. It is evident that the devices designed for laboratory use perform inadequately in mobile operation and that our novel solution enables a significant leap in accuracy.

AI.tldr: A novel GNSS-disciplined oscillator optimized for mobile use (using OCXO with low acceleration sensitivity) achieves <22.6 ns deviation in real-world driving tests vs. up to 2315 ns for state-of-the-art stationary devices.
AI.motivation: Precise synchronization is critical but challenging in mobile scenarios; existing GNSS-disciplined oscillators are designed for stationary operation and perform inadequately under dynamic conditions.
AI.method: The system combines a low-acceleration-sensitivity OCXO with a state-of-the-art GNSS timing module, evaluated via real-world test drives against stationary-optimized equipment.
AI.result: Stationary devices deviated up to 2315 ns; the proposed mobile-optimized system never exceeded 22.6 ns deviation after compensating for stationary offset.
AI.conclusion: Laboratory-grade GNSSDOs are unsuitable for mobile operation; the proposed solution delivers a significant leap in timing accuracy under dynamic conditions.

title: Optimal Planning and Control under Signal Temporal Logic Specifications
summary: This paper addresses the planning and control problem for nonlinear systems under Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications. We first decompose an STL task into finite local tasks. A sampling-based method generates sequences of local waypoints to satisfy all local tasks, from which the corresponding satisfaction pair sets are derived. Following a local-to-global strategy, all sequences of local waypoints are synthesized into a global one, based on which a safe corridor is then constructed. Leveraging the safe corridor and the satisfaction pair sets, an optimization problem is formulated and solved to derive a position trajectory that satisfies the STL task. Finally, numerical examples and comparative results are presented to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: A local-to-global framework for nonlinear systems under STL specifications: decomposes tasks into local subtasks, uses sampling-based waypoint generation and safe corridor construction, then formulates an optimization problem to derive a satisfying position trajectory.
AI.motivation: To address the planning and control problem for nonlinear systems under Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications, which is challenging due to the complexity of temporal-logic constraints coupled with nonlinear dynamics.
AI.method: (1) Decompose STL task into finite local tasks; (2) Use sampling-based method to generate sequences of local waypoints satisfying local tasks, deriving satisfaction pair sets; (3) Synthesize local waypoint sequences into a global sequence via local-to-global strategy; (4) Construct a safe corridor; (5) Formulate and solve an optimization problem using the safe corridor and satisfaction pair sets to obtain a position trajectory.
AI.result: Numerical examples and comparative results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed local-to-global framework with sampling-based waypoint generation and optimization-based trajectory synthesis effectively solves STL-constrained planning and control for nonlinear systems.

title: Graph Neural Ordinary Differential Equations for Power System Identification
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: With the shift towards decentralized energy generation, the increasing complexity of power systems renders physics-based modeling challenging. At the same time the growing amount of available measurement data opens the door for obtaining models in a data-driven manner. A modern method to do so are neural ordinary differential equations (NODEs), offering a framework for continuous time system identification. Recent extensions, so called graph NODEs impose a structural inductive bias that has the potential to improve generalization of the learned representation. In this work, we employ graph NODEs and extend them with novel ideas to develop message-passing graph NODEs (MPG-NODEs) for identification of coupled systems with heterogeneous node dynamics and edge couplings. This encompasses state-of-the-art machine learning architectures to infer latent representations of unmeasured states from past measurements, local node and edge embeddings to account for heterogeneity as well as an autoregressive scheme to allow for piecewise constant control inputs. We apply MPG-NODEs to identify voltage and frequency dynamics of power systems and compare them to a monolith NODE under identical measurement assumptions. Our case study on the IEEE 9-bus system indicates that the proposed MPG-NODE offers a much more flexible framework with transfer learning options that allow to add or remove powerlines and units with little to no retraining.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes message-passing graph neural ordinary differential equations (MPG-NODEs) for data-driven identification of coupled power system dynamics, enabling heterogeneous node/edge modeling and transfer learning across network topologies.
AI.motivation: Decentralized energy generation increases power system complexity, making physics-based modeling difficult. Meanwhile, abundant measurement data enables data-driven modeling. Existing graph NODEs need extensions to handle heterogeneous node dynamics and edge couplings in coupled systems.
AI.method: MPG-NODEs extend graph NODEs with: (1) message-passing mechanisms for coupled system identification, (2) latent representation inference of unmeasured states from past measurements, (3) local node and edge embeddings for heterogeneity, and (4) autoregressive scheme for piecewise constant control inputs.
AI.result: Applied to IEEE 9-bus system for voltage and frequency dynamics identification. MPG-NODEs outperform monolithic NODEs, offering flexible transfer learning that allows adding/removing power lines and units with minimal or no retraining.
AI.conclusion: MPG-NODEs provide a flexible framework for power system identification with superior transfer learning capabilities compared to monolithic NODEs.

title: Toward Low-Altitude Embodied Intelligence: A Sensing-Communication-Computation-Control Closed-Loop Perspective
summary: The rapid growth of the low-altitude economy drives increasingly autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) operations, giving rise to low-altitude embodied intelligence (LAEI), in which sensing, communication, computation, and control (SC$^3$) are tightly integrated to enable closed-loop interaction, ensuring timely, effective, and safe responses in complex or unknown environments. This article systematically explores the LAEI networks, from its fundamental architecture to the diverse scenarios that it can support. We examine key enabling techniques that sustain timely information exchange and effective decision feedback within the $\text{SC}^3$ closed loop. A representative low-altitude UAV mission in an unknown urban area is presented as a case study, where the UAV provides communication services and performs environmental sensing to inform closed-loop control, illustrating how coordinated $\text{SC}^3$ capabilities enable efficient and responsive operation. By identifying major challenges and outlining future research directions, this work serves as a cornerstone for developing next-generation low-altitude intelligent systems.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically explores Low-Altitude Embodied Intelligence (LAEI) networks, integrating sensing, communication, computation, and control (SC³) for closed-loop UAV operations, with a case study in unknown urban environments and future research directions.
AI.motivation: The rapid growth of the low-altitude economy drives increasingly autonomous UAV operations, requiring tight integration of sensing, communication, computation, and control for timely, effective, and safe responses in complex or unknown environments.
AI.method: The paper systematically explores LAEI networks from fundamental architecture to diverse scenarios, examines key enabling techniques for SC³ closed-loop interaction, and presents a representative case study of a low-altitude UAV mission in an unknown urban area.
AI.result: A representative case study demonstrates how coordinated SC³ capabilities enable efficient and responsive UAV operation in unknown urban environments, including providing communication services and performing environmental sensing to inform closed-loop control.
AI.conclusion: By identifying major challenges and outlining future research directions, this work serves as a cornerstone for developing next-generation low-altitude intelligent systems.

title: AI-Native Autonomous Infrastructure (ANAI): A Formal Framework for the Next General-Purpose Technology
comment: 18 pages, 4 figures
summary: Artificial intelligence is increasingly described as a candidate next generation general purpose technology (GPT). However, existing interpretations predominantly emphasize performance scaling rather than structural transformation. This paper introduces a formal framework for evaluating AI as a systemic infrastructural transition rather than merely a computational breakthrough. We propose the concept of AI Native Autonomous Infrastructure (ANAI), defined as a regime in which decision autonomy becomes embedded within critical infrastructures. The framework operationalizes this transition through three quantitative constructs: the Autonomy Index (AIx), the Infrastructure Coupling Coefficient (ICC), and the Technological Transition Potential (TTP). We formalize the joint scaling dynamics of autonomy and infrastructural embedding, derive threshold conditions for paradigm transition, and introduce a phase-space representation of systemic transformation. A temporal transition model further illustrates how nonlinear coevolution between autonomy and infrastructure integration produces super linear growth in transition potential. Unlike prior GPT cycles, the ANAI regime exhibits a recursive energy computation feedback loop in which AI systems both increase computational demand and optimize the infrastructures that sustain them. This feedback mechanism accelerates infrastructural embedding and differentiates AI driven transformation from previous technological revolutions. By shifting analytical focus from model performance to infrastructural autonomy and coupling intensity, this study offers a conceptual and mathematical foundation for assessing whether artificial intelligence constitutes the next general purpose technology.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a formal framework (ANAI) to evaluate AI as a systemic infrastructural transition rather than just a performance-scaled GPT, operationalized via three quantitative constructs (Autonomy Index, Infrastructure Coupling Coefficient, Technological Transition Potential) and a phase-space model showing that recursive energy-computation feedback loops in AI systems produce superlinear growth in transition potential, distinguishing this from prior technological revolutions.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretations of AI as a next-generation GPT overemphasize performance scaling and neglect the structural, infrastructural transformation that AI may induce. The authors seek to shift the analytical focus from model-level capabilities to systemic autonomy and infrastructure coupling.
AI.method: The paper introduces a formal mathematical framework with three quantitative constructs (Autonomy Index AIx, Infrastructure Coupling Coefficient ICC, Technological Transition Potential TTP), a phase-space representation of systemic transformation, and a temporal transition model capturing nonlinear coevolution between autonomy and infrastructure integration.
AI.result: The framework shows that AI-driven transformation exhibits a recursive energy-computation feedback loop—AI systems simultaneously increase computational demand and optimize the infrastructures sustaining them—leading to superlinear growth in transition potential and accelerated infrastructural embedding.
AI.conclusion: By reframing AI's impact through infrastructural autonomy and coupling intensity rather than model performance alone, the paper offers a conceptual and mathematical foundation for assessing whether AI constitutes the next general purpose technology, with the ANAI regime qualitatively differing from prior GPT cycles.

title: A Realistic Discrete Event Simulation model for Ambulance Location and Deployment within a regional Emergency Medical Service
comment: 41 pages, 12 figures
summary: The objective of Emergency Medical Services (EMSs) is to promptly respond to calls from citizens for first aid, providing pre-hospital care and, if necessary, to transfer patients to an appropriate Emergency Department (ED) by ambulance. The efficiency of such a system strongly depends on the deployment of ambulance home bases, i.e., locations where ambulances and their crews are strategically positioned, ready to respond to emergency calls. This paper presents a general Discrete Event Simulation (DES) model designed to capture the stochastic behaviour and workflow of regional ambulance emergency systems. The proposed model incorporates and integrates information collected from different sources, reproducing very accurately the operation of the ambulance system, thus allowing a more comprehensive and realistic analysis. To show the applicability and reliability of the proposed general model, a case study provided by the Azienda Regionale Emergenza Sanitaria - ARES 118 (an Italian Regional Emergency Medical Services Authority - ARES~118}) is presented. It concerns a territory within the Lazio region of Italy, including a medium-size city along with sparsely populated areas. The reported results about scenario analyses highlight how the model we propose can be fruitfully used by the managers to improve effectiveness and quickness of the entire regional EMS system.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a Discrete Event Simulation (DES) model for Emergency Medical Services (EMS) that captures stochastic behavior and workflow of ambulance systems, validated through a case study in Italy's Lazio region to help managers improve system effectiveness and response times.
AI.motivation: The efficiency of EMS systems depends heavily on the strategic deployment of ambulance home bases, and there is a need for a comprehensive, realistic simulation model to analyze and improve such systems.
AI.method: A general Discrete Event Simulation (DES) model is developed that integrates information from multiple sources to reproduce the stochastic behavior and workflow of regional ambulance emergency systems.
AI.result: A case study in the Lazio region of Italy (including a medium-size city and sparsely populated areas) demonstrates the model's ability to accurately reproduce system operations and support scenario analyses.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DES model can be effectively used by EMS managers to improve the effectiveness and quickness of entire regional EMS systems.

title: The Fragility of Learning LQG Controllers
summary: Learning methods are increasingly used to synthesize controllers from data, yet existing sample-complexity characterizations for continuous control are sharp only in the fully observed setting. This paper studies the partially observed case by deriving information-theoretic lower bounds for learning Linear Quadratic Gaussian (LQG) controllers from offline trajectories generated by a (linear) exploration policy. We prove an $\varepsilon$-local minimax excess-cost lower bound that applies to any algorithm mapping the offline dataset to a stabilizing linear controller. The bound is expressed in terms of the Hessian of the LQG cost with respect to model parameters and the inverse Fisher Information induced by the exploration policy. We further provide system-theoretic characterizations of these objects, enabling transparent construction of hard instances. Instantiating the bound on classical fragile robust-control examples, including variants of the Doyle LQG fragility counterexample and non-minimum-phase systems, demonstrates when fragile robust control problems translate into high sample complexity for learning-enabled control. These results suggest the asymptotic optimality of certainty-equivalent synthesis and motivate the importance of both task-directed experiment design and system co-design for sample-efficient learning in partially observed control.

AI.tldr: This paper derives information-theoretic lower bounds for learning LQG controllers from offline data in partially observed settings, showing that fragile robust control problems lead to high sample complexity.
AI.motivation: Existing sample-complexity bounds for continuous control are sharp only in fully observed settings; this paper addresses the gap for partially observed (LQG) control.
AI.method: The authors prove an ε-local minimax excess-cost lower bound expressed via the Hessian of the LQG cost and the inverse Fisher Information from the exploration policy, with system-theoretic characterizations for constructing hard instances.
AI.result: Instantiations on Doyle's LQG fragility counterexample and non-minimum-phase systems show that fragile robust control problems translate into high sample complexity.
AI.conclusion: The results suggest asymptotic optimality of certainty-equivalent synthesis and highlight the need for task-directed experiment design and system co-design.

title: Reduced-Order Data Assimilation for Thermospheric Density Using Physics-informed SINDyc Models
summary: Accurate estimation of thermospheric mass density is a prerequisite for orbit prediction and space situational awareness, where the upper atmosphere responds nonlinearly to solar and geomagnetic forcing across several orders of magnitude. Physics-based general circulation models resolve this response but are computationally expensive, while empirical models run cheaply but lack a time-evolving atmospheric state. This work couples a data-driven reduced-order thermospheric model with a Kalman filter that assimilates in situ density observations. An autoregressive Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics with control (SINDy$_c$-AR) reduced-order model derived from the Thermosphere-Ionosphere-Electrodynamics General Circulation Model (TIE-GCM) captures the dominant modes of variability and their dependence on solar and geomagnetic drivers at a fraction of the parent model's cost. Density observations from CHAMP, GRACE, GRACE-FO, GOCE, and Swarm are assimilated across a range of orbital configurations and geomagnetic conditions, with a linear DMDc model evaluated as a reference. Assimilation reduces density estimation error relative to open-loop predictions, most visibly during geomagnetic storms and under single-satellite coverage. SINDy$_c$-AR and DMDc perform comparably on assimilated orbits; on withheld orbits, SINDy$_c$-AR is more accurate in the in-training scenarios while DMDc is better in the out-of-training 2024 Swarm-C case. Benchmarks against NRLMSIS~2.1 and HASDM (2000--2019, where available) show that empirical references can outperform the assimilated model far from the assimilated track, so results are framed as improvements over the open-loop forecast.

AI.tldr: A data-driven reduced-order thermospheric model (SINDy$_c$-AR) derived from TIE-GCM is coupled with a Kalman filter to assimilate in situ density observations from multiple satellites, reducing density estimation errors compared to open-loop predictions, especially during geomagnetic storms.
AI.motivation: Accurate thermospheric mass density estimation is critical for orbit prediction and space situational awareness, but existing approaches face a trade-off: physics-based models are computationally expensive, while empirical models lack time-evolving atmospheric states.
AI.method: Couples a SINDy$_c$-AR reduced-order model (derived from TIE-GCM) with a Kalman filter to assimilate in situ density observations from CHAMP, GRACE, GRACE-FO, GOCE, and Swarm; DMDc is used as a reference model.
AI.result: Assimilation reduces density estimation error over open-loop predictions, especially during geomagnetic storms. SINDy$_c$-AR and DMDc perform comparably on assimilated orbits; SINDy$_c$-AR is more accurate in-training, DMDc better in the out-of-training 2024 Swarm-C case. Empirical references can outperform the assimilated model far from the assimilated track.
AI.conclusion: The proposed data-driven assimilation framework improves thermospheric density estimation, but performance degrades far from assimilated orbits, highlighting the need for broader observational coverage.

title: Reachability Analysis of the State Transition and State Covariance Matrices for an LTV System
comment: 12 pages, 2 figures
summary: In this paper, we study the reachability of two closely related matrices appearing in the analysis of linear time-varying (LTV) systems over a finite time interval, namely, its closed-loop state transition matrix via a state feedback control and its state covariance matrix starting from some given initial state covariance matrix. Under a mild assumption, we first characterize the set of closed-loop terminal state transition matrices reachable from the identity matrix using controls of the state feedback form. Then, we provide the set of terminal state covariance matrices reachable from any given positive definite initial state covariance matrix when the LTV system is not necessarily controllable. Both results are based on the solutions of corresponding matrix Riccati differential equations (RDE).

AI.tldr: This paper characterizes reachable sets of closed-loop state transition matrices and state covariance matrices for linear time-varying systems over finite time intervals, using matrix Riccati differential equations, without requiring controllability.
AI.motivation: To characterize the reachable sets of two key matrices (closed-loop state transition matrix via state feedback, and state covariance matrix) for LTV systems under mild assumptions, extending prior results that often require controllability.
AI.method: The authors employ matrix Riccati differential equations (RDE) to derive the reachable sets of (1) closed-loop terminal state transition matrices from the identity using state-feedback controls, and (2) terminal state covariance matrices from any positive definite initial covariance, without requiring the LTV system to be controllable.
AI.result: Explicit characterization of reachable sets for both the closed-loop terminal state transition matrix (via state feedback) and the terminal state covariance matrix, under mild assumptions and without controllability requirements.
AI.conclusion: The reachable sets of both matrices can be fully characterized via solutions of matrix Riccati differential equations, even when the LTV system is not controllable, generalizing existing controllability-dependent results.

title: Exploiting Differential Flatness for Efficient Learning-based Model Predictive Control of Constrained Multi-Input Control Affine Systems
comment: Accepted for publication in 2026 European Control Conference
summary: Learning-based control techniques use data from past trajectories to control systems with uncertain dynamics. However, learning-based controllers are often computationally inefficient, limiting their practicality. To address this limitation, we propose a learning-based controller that exploits differential flatness, a property of many robotic systems. Recent research on using flatness for learning-based control either is limited in that it (i) ignores input constraints, (ii) applies only to single-input systems, or (iii) is tailored to specific platforms. In contrast, our approach uses a system extension and block-diagonal cost formulation to control general multi-input, nonlinear, affine systems. Furthermore, it satisfies input and half-space flat state constraints and guarantees probabilistic Lyapunov decrease using only two sequential convex optimizations. We show that our approach performs similarly to, but is multiple times more efficient than, a Gaussian process model predictive controller in simulation, and achieves competitive tracking in real hardware experiments.

AI.tldr: A computationally efficient learning-based controller using differential flatness that handles multi-input nonlinear affine systems with input and state constraints via two sequential convex optimizations, outperforming GP-MPC in efficiency with similar performance.
AI.motivation: Learning-based controllers are often computationally inefficient, limiting their practicality in real-world deployment.
AI.method: Exploits differential flatness with system extension and block-diagonal cost formulation to control general multi-input, nonlinear, affine systems using only two sequential convex optimizations.
AI.result: Achieves similar performance to GP-MPC but with multiple times higher efficiency in simulation, and competitive tracking in real hardware experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed flatness-based learning controller is computationally efficient while satisfying input and state constraints, making it practical for real-time robotic control.

title: Data-Driven Privacy-Preserving Modeling and Frequency Regulation with Aggregated Electric Vehicles via Bilinear Hidden Markov Model
comment: 12 Pages, 10 figures, Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid
summary: Vehicle-to-Grid (V2G) technology allows bidirectional power flow for real-time grid support, making electric vehicles (EVs) well-suited for ancillary services such as frequency regulation. However, existing methods for flexibility estimation and coordinating aggregated EVs often rely on individual EV traveling information (e.g., arrival/departure time) and/or characteristic parameters (e.g., charging efficiency, battery capacity) as well as real-time state-of-charge (SOC), which raises privacy concerns and faces data quality issues. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a data-driven, privacy-preserving modeling and control framework for frequency regulation using aggregated EVs. AI.tldr: This paper proposes a data-driven, privacy-preserving framework for frequency regulation using aggregated EVs that estimates power outputs and flexibility without requiring individual EV information, outperforming model-based and federated learning methods under SOC data inaccuracies.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for flexibility estimation and coordinated control of aggregated EVs rely on individual EV traveling information (e.g., arrival/departure time), characteristic parameters (e.g., charging efficiency, battery capacity), and real-time SOC, which raises privacy concerns and faces data quality issues.
AI.method: A data-driven, privacy-preserving modeling and control framework that estimates power outputs and flexibility of aggregated EVs for frequency regulation without requiring any individual EV information.
AI.result: Simulation results validate the accuracy and effectiveness of the proposed method, which outperforms model-based and federated learning-based methods under SOC data inaccuracies.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables effective frequency regulation while preserving user privacy and ensuring practical scalability, addressing both privacy concerns and data quality issues inherent in existing approaches.
